463.title: Pranayama (2.49–2.53)
463.hook: with the seat settled, the breath is next, and Patanjali says it thins the covering over the mind's light
463.tomorrow: Pratyahara — the senses follow the mind home
463.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama as part of daily worship, for instance before reciting the Gayatri mantra in the morning, and yoga teachers usually introduce breath retention gradually and under supervision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asana, the seat, steady and comfortable. Three words, and that's all it says.

You step out of a hot shower and the bathroom mirror is solid white. You could scrub it with a towel and leave streaks. Or you could open the door a crack, let the air move, and wait. Slowly, from the edges in, the fog lifts, and there you are. You didn't put your face back in the mirror. It was there the whole time. Patanjali's fourth limb works on the breath, and the reason he gives for it sounds a lot like that mirror.
screen: `A FOGGED MIRROR.` → `DON'T SCRUB. LET THE AIR MOVE.` → `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Prana is life breath, the energy that moves in breathing. The second part of the word is read two ways: ayama, stretching out, or yama, reining in. Teachers have used both, and both fit. Sutra 2.49: once the seat is settled, pranayama is the pausing of the flow of in-breath and out-breath. Sutra 2.50: the breath can be outer, inner, or held still, measured by place, time and number, and it becomes, in his words, long and subtle. Not forceful. Not heroic. Long and fine, like thread. Sutra 2.51 adds a fourth kind, beyond outer and inner, where the breath seems to settle on its own. Then the reason, in 2.52: from this, the covering over the light thins away. The light is the mind's clarity. It was never missing, only covered. The classical commentary says the covering is the karma that hides discernment, and repeats an old saying: there is no discipline higher than pranayama; it burns away impurity and lets the light of knowledge shine. Finally 2.53: the mind becomes fit for concentration. Pranayama isn't the destination. It gets the mind ready for the inner limbs. A practical note: strong breath-holding is something people learn in person, with a teacher, and none of it is needed here. What anyone can do is what 2.50 points to: let the breath get a little longer, a little finer.
screen: `PRANA: THE LIFE BREATH.` · `LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `THE COVERING OVER THE LIGHT THINS.` · `THE MIND GROWS FIT TO FOCUS.` · then, large: `THE VEIL THINS.`

segments.voice: Sit steady and easy, and let each out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, with no strain and no holding. Make the breath so quiet you could barely hear it, and if you ever feel short of air, go back to normal breathing. Then watch the mind, and notice whether anything clears.
Pranayama. Working with the life breath, letting it grow long and subtle, the fourth limb of yoga.
Your line: the veil thins. The light was never gone; it was only covered. Until tomorrow.

464.title: Pratyahara — the senses follow the mind home (2.54–2.55)
464.hook: the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses settle with it, like bees following their leader home
464.howItsDone: In yoga practice, pratyahara is usually cultivated by resting attention on one object, such as the breath or a mantra, until the senses quiet; teachers often cite the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs as the classic image.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranayama. The breath grows long and subtle, and the veil over the light thins.

Try to stop hearing the fridge hum. Really try. Clench, focus, tell your ears to quit. It gets louder. Now remember the last time you were lost in a great book or a deep conversation. The fridge was humming then too. You didn't hear it. Nobody told your ears to stop. Your attention went somewhere, and your ears simply followed it. Patanjali's answer to the noisy senses isn't to fight them. It's to move the mind, and let the senses follow.
screen: `TRY NOT TO HEAR THE FRIDGE.` → `IT GETS LOUDER.` → `LOST IN A BOOK, IT'S GONE.`

segments.voice: Prati means back, toward. Ahara means taking in, even food. Pratyahara: drawing back, withdrawal. Sutra 2.54: when the senses aren't joined to their objects, they take on, as it were, the nature of the mind itself. The classical commentary gives the picture. A swarm of bees follows its leader, which the commentary calls the king of the bees. When the leader flies up, they all fly up. When it settles, they all settle. So with the senses and the mind. Restrain the mind, and the senses come home on their own. You don't chase each bee. Sutra 2.55: from this, supreme mastery of the senses. The commentary lists other views, enjoying only what's allowed, or using the senses without being hooked, and then says the highest is this: when the mind is one-pointed, the senses don't go out at all. The Bhagavad Gita has a neighbor image, the tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell. Pratyahara is the hinge of the eight. The first five limbs face outward: others, yourself, body, breath, senses. The last three face inward. And book two ends here. Look at its road: kriya yoga, discipline, study, surrender. The five afflictions, from not seeing to the fear of death. Karma's storehouse. Suffering, its cause, and its cure, discernment. Then the outer limbs, one by one. All of it, a way of calling the bees home.

segments.voice: Give the mind one place to rest: the feeling of the breath at the tip of the nose. Don't try to block sounds or sights; when a noise pulls you, just return to the breath. Notice whether the hearing quiets a little on its own, following the mind.
Pratyahara. The drawing back of the senses, the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses follow it home.
Your line: withdrawal. Settle the leader, and the swarm comes home. Day four sixty-four, done.

465.title: Concentration, meditation, absorption (3.1–3.3)
465.hook: book three opens with the three inner limbs in three short sutras: hold the mind in one place, let it flow, then disappear into what you're seeing
465.howItsDone: In Hindu meditation traditions, practitioners often fix attention on a point such as the heart, the space between the eyebrows, a sacred image or a mantra, and teachers describe concentration deepening into meditation and absorption over long practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pratyahara, withdrawal. The senses follow the mind home, like bees following their leader, and book two closed.

The teacher Drona sets a wooden bird high in a tree and calls his students to aim. In a story often told from the Mahabharata, he asks each one before he shoots: what do you see? One sees the tree, the branches, the sky, his brothers. Drona sends him away. Then Arjuna steps up. What do you see? The bird. Describe the bird. I see only its head. Shoot. Popular retellings make it the eye; the epic says the head. Book three of the Yoga Sutras is called Vibhuti, the book of powers. But it opens with Arjuna's kind of seeing, in three steps.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `ONLY ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.1: dharana, concentration, is binding the mind to one place. The classical commentary lists places: the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or something outside the body. Dharana comes from a root meaning to hold, the same root as dharma. You hold the mind there, the way you'd hold a cup steady. It slips. You bring it back. That's dharana. Sutra 3.2: dhyana, meditation, is when the idea of that object flows on without a break. One thread, no knots. A later image some teachers use: oil poured from one jar to another, a single unbroken stream. Sutra 3.3: samadhi, absorption, is that same flow when only the object shines, as if empty of its own form. In dhyana, there's still you, meditating on something. In samadhi, the sense of me meditating drops away. Only the bird's head. Arjuna in the story isn't thinking, I'm concentrating well. There's just the target. These aren't three separate techniques. They're one movement, deepening. Hold. Flow. Disappear into it. There's an everyday version: being so absorbed in a song, a game, a sick child's breathing, that the self drops out of view. Patanjali's claim is that this can be trained, and pointed at the deepest things.
screen: `DHARANA: HOLD THE MIND IN ONE PLACE.` · `DHYANA: AN UNBROKEN FLOW.` · `SAMADHI: ONLY THE OBJECT SHINES.` · `ONE MOVEMENT, DEEPENING.` · then, large: `DHARANA, DHYANA, SAMADHI.`

segments.voice: Choose one place, the tip of the nose where the breath touches or the center of the chest, and hold the mind there; when it slips, and it will, bring it back without scolding. That's dharana. If for a few breaths it stays without your holding, notice the flow: a taste of dhyana.
Concentration. Dharana, binding the mind to one place, the first of the three inner limbs, which deepen into meditation and absorption.
Your line: dharana, dhyana, samadhi. Book three opens with seeing only the target. Rest well.

466.title: The three together (3.4–3.8)
466.hook: concentration, meditation and absorption on one object get a single name, samyama, the tool the rest of book three is built on
466.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras present samyama as the combined practice of the three inner limbs on a single object, learned gradually over years, and they stress that its insights are steps toward liberation rather than the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: concentration, meditation, absorption. Hold the mind, let it flow, and disappear into it.

Watch someone braid hair. Three strands, each one loose and floppy on its own. Left over middle. Right over middle. Again, again. Somewhere along the way, three strands stop being three strands. They become one braid, strong enough to hold its shape all day. Nobody would call it three things anymore. Patanjali braids the three inner limbs, and the braid gets its own name, a name that will carry the rest of book three.

Sutra 3.4: the three together are samyama. Sam means together. Yama you already know, from the first limb: reining in, holding. Samyama, holding together. Concentration, meditation and absorption, all on the same object, at once. From here on, whenever Patanjali says, by samyama on this, that happens, this is the tool he means. Sutra 3.5: by mastering it, the light of insight. Prajna, wisdom, begins to shine. Sutra 3.6: it's applied in stages. You don't jump to the top. The classical commentary adds a striking line here: yoga is to be known by yoga, and yoga grows out of yoga. Each stage, practiced, opens the next. Then inside and outside. Sutra 3.7: these three are inner, compared with the five limbs before: the restraints, the observances, the seat, the breath, the senses drawing back. And then 3.8, the humbling line: even these are outer, compared with the seedless. Remember seedless samadhi, from the end of book one? Absorption with no object at all, no seed left to sprout. Measured against that, even the braid is still on the outside. So samyama is powerful, and Patanjali is about to spend most of a book on what it can do. But he's said up front: it isn't the end of the road.

Prajna, wisdom's light, which begins to shine when samyama is mastered: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object at once, the tool of book three.
Your line: samyama. Three strands, one object, one braid that holds. That's day four sixty-six.

467.title: The transformations of mind (3.9–3.15)
467.hook: even stillness is a kind of change, and the same mark can mean one, ten or a hundred depending on where it stands
467.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study the transformations of 3.9–3.15 with the classical commentary, and in meditation practitioners watch thoughts arise and fade as a way of seeing change clearly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajna and samyama: concentration, meditation and absorption braided on one thing, and wisdom's light begins to shine.

Write the number one on a piece of paper. A single upright stroke. Now put a zero after it. Same stroke, same ink, and it means ten. Add another zero: a hundred. The stroke didn't grow. Nothing about it changed, and yet what it means changed completely, just by where it stands. The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras uses this very example, to explain how things change, including the mind.
screen: `ONE STROKE OF A PEN.` → `ONE, TEN, A HUNDRED.` → `THE STROKE NEVER CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The word is parinama: transformation, change of form. Patanjali starts with the mind. Sutra 3.9: even stillness is a change. A scattering impression fades, a stilling impression rises, and the mind shifts toward quiet. Sutra 3.10: practiced again and again, that shift becomes a calm, steady flow. Then 3.11: scatteredness wanes, one-pointedness rises. And 3.12: the thought that fades and the thought that rises become alike, the same object, moment after moment. That's one-pointedness, described as a kind of change. Then he widens the lens. Sutra 3.13: the same three changes run through everything, the elements and the senses too: change of property, change of time, change of condition. Besides the stroke of the pen, the commentary gives another picture: the same woman is called mother, daughter and sister, depending on who's speaking. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath: the substance that carries the properties, past, present and still to come. And 3.15: a different order produces a different change. The commentary's example is clay. A lump becomes a pot. The pot breaks into shards. The shards become dust. The clay is there the whole way through. Why put this in a book on meditation? Because to do samyama on anything, you need to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does.

Parinama, change of form. Even stillness and one-pointedness are changes, carried by something that stays.

468.title: Knowledge of past and future (3.16)
468.hook: the first of the powers in book three follows straight from yesterday: see how a thing changes, all the way, and you see where it came from and where it's going
468.howItsDone: The siddhis of Yoga Sutras book three are studied in yoga lineages as signs of mastery; Hindu stories describe sages who know past and future, and teachers often caution students not to make such powers their goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parinama, what changes. Lump, pot, shards, and the clay all the way through.

A forester cuts a slice from a fallen oak and counts the rings. This thin one, a dry year. This dark scar, a fire. These wide ones, good rain. She can read a century of weather in a circle of wood. Ask her, and she can tell you something about the years ahead too: how this stand of trees will grow, which ones will need light. She isn't psychic. She just understands, deeply, how wood changes. The powers of book three begin with one that sounds like her.
screen: `A SLICE OF OAK.` → `A DRY YEAR, A FIRE, GOOD RAIN.` → `THE POWERS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of the past and the future. Remember the three: change of property, change of time, change of condition. The future pot hidden in the clay, the past lump still in the pot. If concentration, meditation and absorption rest fully on how a thing changes, the whole arc opens up: where it's been, where it's heading. The word for past is atita, what has gone by. Future is anagata, what has not yet come. You heard anagata a couple of weeks ago, in the pain not yet come, to be avoided. The word for these powers in general is siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection, and this is the first of a long list: knowing other minds, strength, the inner map of the body, and stranger things. How are they meant? The classical commentators take them as real capacities that come with deep practice, and the stories of sages tell of them. Some readers take them more inwardly, as pictures of what clear seeing makes possible. The sutras list them plainly, without bragging, and before the list is done they'll add a warning, heard in its place. For now, notice how ordinary the first power's logic is. It isn't magic fire. It's the forester's eye, taken all the way: understanding change so completely that time opens in both directions.

469.title: Knowledge of others' minds (3.19)
469.hook: samyama on another person's state of mind reveals that mind, and the very next sutra draws a line around what it can't see
469.howItsDone: Many Hindu stories describe sages who know the minds of those who come to them, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras point to 3.20's limit and to the yamas as the frame in which any such power is held.

segments.voice: Yesterday: siddhi, and the powers begin. See how a thing changes, all the way, and time opens in both directions.

Your phone buzzes. It's your oldest friend. One word: hey. No punctuation. And somehow you already know something's wrong. Not what. Just that. You've read a thousand of their heys, and this one is different. Nobody calls that a superpower. It's what close attention to one person, for years, starts to do. Patanjali names a power that sounds like a much bigger version of that. And then, immediately, he tells you exactly where it stops.
screen: `ONE WORD: HEY.` → `SOMETHING'S WRONG.` → `NOT WHAT. JUST THAT.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.19: by samyama on the idea in another's mind, knowledge of that other mind. The word is pratyaya, the content of awareness at a given moment, the mood or idea running through it. Rest concentration, meditation and absorption on that, and the other person's state of mind becomes clear: troubled, calm, grasping, glad. Then comes the warning, in the very next line. Sutra 3.20: but not its object. You can know that the mind is angry, but not what it's angry at, because that wasn't the object of the samyama. The classical commentary is careful here. The power reaches the color of the mind, not its whole story. Even at its height, knowing another person has a limit, and the sutra writes the limit right into the power. Notice the order of the book, too. Patanjali didn't open with powers. He opened with non-harm, truth, not stealing. Anyone who reads a mind is standing very close to someone else's inner life, and the first limb has already said how to stand there. Now the week, from the top. Pranayama, the veil thins. Pratyahara, the senses follow the mind home. Concentration, meditation, absorption. Prajna, samyama. The transformations, what changes. Past and future. And today, other minds, with a line drawn around them. A week that went inward, and now begins to turn outward again, toward what that inward work can do.
